about: Checks and lessons that Softanza Radar shows beside each entry, keyed by entry id. Written by the desk with each weekly survey.

build.why: Is the agent's local permission file tracked in this repository?
Was it ever committed, even if it is gone today?
Keep it out of every clone, not only your machine. This one writes: it adds a line to .gitignore.
Name a secret in a command, never type it.

2026-11-08-agent-approvals-leak-secrets.lesson: A coding agent asks before it runs a command. When you approve a command for good, it remembers the exact text of that command, so it can recognise it next time. If the command contained a password, the password is now stored in a plain file inside your project. Files in a project tend to get committed and published. The cure is to keep secrets out of commands: put them in environment variables and write their names.
terms: the commands an agent may run without asking
a named value the shell keeps outside your files
replace a secret with a new one after it leaked
quiz: Why does deleting the file not fix a leak that was pushed?
Git keeps every earlier version, and forks and clones keep their own copies. The secret must be replaced, which is called rotating it.
What should a command contain instead of a password?
A reference such as $DATABASE_URL, so the stored rule records the name and not the value.

build.why: Find places where code is chosen by a name read from text.
The safe shape: tools come from a registry written in code.
build.cmd:
TOOLS = {"search": search, "summarise": summarise}
fn = TOOLS[name]   # a name outside the registry raises KeyError

2026-11-08-tool-paths-from-prompts-run-c.lesson: An agent's tools are functions. If the agent finds which function to run by reading a name or a path from a prompt or a file, then whoever writes that text chooses which code runs. The safe pattern is a registry: the program lists its tools in code, and text may only pick among them.
terms: loading code by a name known only at run time
a fixed table that maps names to the functions allowed
quiz: Who controls the code that runs when a tool path comes from a template?
Whoever can write the template: a shared prompt store, a fetched file, or a user's input.

build.why: Which mcp-go version does your Go module use? 1.2.1 carries the fix.
The rule a client follows before asking for a token.
build.cmd:
if metadata.resource != configured_server_url:
    refuse("server declared another resource")

2026-11-08-mcp-oauth-resource-check.lesson: When an MCP server needs you to sign in, it tells your client which resource the token is for. A dishonest server can name a different, legitimate server. If the client believes it, your sign-in produces a token for that other server, and the dishonest one receives it. The client must check that the resource named is the server it actually connected to.
terms: Model Context Protocol, how agents connect to tool servers
the field that says which server a token is for
using someone's valid token somewhere it was not meant for
quiz: What does the client compare before requesting a token?
The resource the server declares, against the server URL the client was configured with.

build.why: Does any workflow here use the event?

2026-11-08-github-blocks-pull-request-ta.lesson: GitHub Actions can run a workflow when someone opens a pull request. The pull_request_target event runs it with the main repository's secrets, even for a pull request from a stranger's fork. If that workflow runs the stranger's code, the code can take the secrets. GitHub now blocks the event by default in public repositories.
terms: a copy of a repository under another account
an automated job that GitHub runs on events
quiz: Why is running fork code under pull_request_target risky?
It runs with the base repository's secrets, so outside code can read them.

build.why: Which Zig builds your project today?
Try the new release on a branch, with capped parallelism.

2026-11-08-zig-0-17-1.lesson: Zig is the language Softanza's engine is written in. A minor version of Zig can change the language and its standard library, so moving two minor versions is a project: build on a branch, count what breaks, then plan.
terms: the middle number, 0.17 in 0.17.1; in Zig it may change the language
something that worked before and broke in a new release
quiz: Why measure on a branch first?
So the count of what breaks is known before anyone commits to the move.

build.why: The admission rule in a few lines: where did the target come from?

2026-11-08-spillway-target-admission.lesson: Prompt injection hides instructions in text an agent reads, such as an email. SPILLWAY does not try to recognise every trick. It asks one plain question about each action: did its target, such as a recipient or a payee, come from the user's request or from a trusted, typed field? If it came from free text, the action is refused.
terms: instructions hidden in data an AI reads
an action that changes something: send, pay, delete
quiz: What does SPILLWAY check that a list of allowed tools does not?
Where an action's target came from, not only which tool is called.

build.why: Add one test that exercises the documented change, with the answer taken from the old version.
build.cmd:
# expected output recorded on the OLD runtime
expected = run_on_old_runtime(edge_input)
assert repaired(edge_input) == expected

2026-11-08-llm-repairs-pass-wrong.lesson: When an API changes, an AI can repair code so that it runs without errors and still gives wrong answers. Tests with ordinary inputs miss this. One input chosen from the change note, with the right answer taken from the old program, catches most wrong repairs.
terms: a test that pins behaviour so a change cannot alter it unseen
an input chosen to hit the exact case that changed
quiz: Where should the expected answer for the edge input come from?
From the old program on the old runtime, not from the model that wrote the repair.

build.why: Check a feed file against Radar's key.
build.cmd:
curl -sO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mayouni/stzradar/main/feed/index.json
curl -sO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mayouni/stzradar/main/feed/index.json.sig
curl -sO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mayouni/stzradar/main/keys/allowed_signers
ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I feed@radar -n radar-feed -s index.json.sig < index.json

2026-11-08-feed-signing.lesson: A signature lets a reader check that a file is exactly what its publisher signed. Radar signs its feed with one key and publishes the public half. Your tool checks the signature and the key's fingerprint before it shows a single notice.
terms: the half of a key pair anyone may hold to check signatures
a short hash that names one key
quiz: Why pin the fingerprint in your own code?
A key fetched beside the feed only proves the two agree; a pinned fingerprint proves it is Radar's key.

build.why: Every entry touching one area, from the terminal.

2026-11-08-lookout-opens.lesson: Radar reads developments in AI at their source and writes each one twice: as a page for people and as data for programs. The data is a feed any tool can read, filtered by who you are and how urgent the matter is.
terms: a file of entries that programs fetch and read
who a notice is written for: developer, user, learner, maintainer
quiz: What is the difference between level and relevance?
Relevance says how much it touches Softanza; level says how much it asks of the reader.

build.why: Copy the watch to start your own. This one writes: it creates a folder.
See everything that belongs to a project: one file.
After editing it, let the check name anything missing or wrong, line by line.
Make the key that signs your feed, outside the repository. This one writes: it creates the key pair.

2026-11-09-lookout-for-any-project.lesson: A tool built for one project usually hides that project everywhere in its code: names, addresses, texts. Radar gathered all of it into one file, radar.yaml, and the tools read that file instead. Changing the file changes the whole watch: what its agent studies, what it reads, who it writes for, and what the site and the bar show. The parts every watch shares, like the feed's fields and its signature, stay the same, so one reader works for all of them.
terms: a file that says how a tool should behave for one project, read by the tool instead of written into its code
a plain-text format for configuration: keys, values and lists, laid out by indentation
write into your page the one key you trust, so a feed signed by any other key is refused
quiz: Why keep the project's names in one file rather than in the tools?
So that another project changes one file, and the tools, the feed, the site and the bar follow without any edit to their code.
Why does the bar take the key from the page that includes it?
The page's owner decides which watch they trust. If the key came with the feed, anyone serving a feed could also serve a matching key.

build.why: Run the 4 GB model locally with llama.cpp and talk to it in the terminal. This downloads about 4 GB.
Serve it on your machine with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so your own agent can call it.
Judge it on your own questions, not on the vendor's table: keep a file of cases with the answers you expect, and score both models on it.

2026-11-11-nemotron-bolt-e4b.lesson: A small language model is one that fits on an ordinary computer. Bolt E4B is about 4 GB once its numbers are stored in 4 bits instead of 16, which is called quantization. NVIDIA took Google's Gemma 4 model and trained it further with reinforcement learning, rewarding it when it called tools correctly and followed instructions. Its scores are NVIDIA's own; a project that wants to use it measures it on its own work first.
terms: storing a model's numbers with fewer bits, so it takes less memory
the file format llama.cpp and similar runtimes load models from
training a finished model further, for a particular kind of work
quiz: Why are Bolt E4B's benchmark scores marked as claimed?
They were measured by NVIDIA, which made the model; a user's own test on their own work is the measurement that counts for them.
What does 8B parameters, 4B effective mean?
The file holds 8 billion numbers, but the model uses about 4 billion of them for each token, so it runs at the cost of a 4B model.

build.why: Render each PDF page to an image first: the model reads pages as pictures. This writes PNG files.
Keep a few pages whose correct text you typed yourself, and compare any reader's output with them.

2026-11-11-nemotron-parse.lesson: OCR turns the picture of a page into text. Older pipelines do it in steps: find the lines, read each one, then guess the order. Nemotron 3.5 Parse does all of it in one small model and also says which block is a table, a chart or a title, and where it sits. It can look a second time at tables and charts to read them better, which costs time and gains accuracy.
terms: optical character recognition: reading the text in an image
the order in which a person would read the blocks of a page
the rectangle that encloses one block on the page
quiz: Why does a triple pass read tables better than a single pass?
It finds the tables and charts first, then reads each one again at higher detail, and merges the result back.
What should you compare a new OCR model against?
Pages from your own documents whose correct text you know, in the languages and scripts your users write.

build.why: Measure retrieval with your own questions: for each question, list the page that answers it, then count how often the model ranks it first.
A shorter vector costs less to store. Truncate, then normalise again, then measure again.

2026-11-11-nemotron-embed-1b.lesson: An embedding model turns a text or an image into a list of numbers, a vector, so that things with similar meaning get similar vectors. Search then means finding the vectors closest to the question's vector. Nemotron 3.5 Embed can embed the picture of a page, so a typed question can find a chart or a table, and it was trained for many languages.
terms: a vector of numbers that stands for the meaning of a text or an image
finding the documents that answer a question
scale a vector to length one, so only its direction counts
quiz: Why test a multilingual model on Arabic and French items, not only English?
A model that ranks first in English can rank lower in other languages; only items in those languages show it.
What changes when you keep only the first 512 dimensions of a vector?
It takes less memory and search is faster, at some cost in accuracy, which you measure.

build.why: Run a model with its small drafter in llama.cpp and compare tokens per second with and without it.
Check the answers are identical with the drafter on and off, at temperature 0: speculative decoding must change speed only.

2026-11-11-speculative-decoding-dflash.lesson: A language model writes one token at a time, and each token costs a full pass through the model. Speculative decoding lets a much smaller model guess the next few tokens quickly; the big model then checks all the guesses in one pass and keeps the ones it agrees with. The text is the same as without the guesser, and it arrives sooner when the guesses are often right.
terms: a piece of a word, the unit a language model reads and writes
the small model that guesses tokens for the large one to check
reading the prompt before the first token is written
quiz: Why does the drafter need the same tokenizer as the main model?
The main model checks the drafter's tokens directly, so both must cut text into the same pieces.
Does speculative decoding change the answer?
No: the main model keeps only the tokens it would have written itself, so only the speed changes.

build.why: Run the 1 GB text model locally with llama.cpp. This downloads the model.
Ask a choice question by probability, not by generation: score each option's tokens after the prompt and keep the most likely.
build.cmd: for option in ["billing", "shipping", "technical"]: score[option] = logprob(prompt + option)

build.why: Several questions about one long input: read the input once and keep its cache, then ask each question from that cache.
build.cmd: state = model.prefill(ticket); answers = [state.ask(q) for q in questions]

2026-11-11-liquid-lfm3.lesson: A small model can be asked to write an answer, or to say how likely each allowed answer is. The second is often more reliable, because the model cannot wander off the list. Liquid AI's d1 models take this further: they read one input once and answer a whole list of questions about it, each with a probability you can trust as a probability. LFM3 is also built for small devices: most of its layers are cheap convolutions, with attention kept for long context.
terms: one run of the model over its input, the unit of its cost
a probability that matches how often the answer is right: 0.8 means right about 8 times in 10
reading the input before answering, often the largest cost for a long input
quiz: Why can reading by probability beat generation for a choice question?
The model only ranks the allowed options, so it cannot answer outside the list or phrase the answer in a way the program misreads.
What does a shared prefill save when you ask five questions about one ticket?
The ticket is read once instead of five times; only the short questions are read again.

build.why: Measure how long your model takes to read a fixed prompt before it answers: that is the prefill a saved state would skip.
llama.cpp can save the state after a prompt and load it next time. This writes a state file.
Check the restored state gives the same answer as reading the prompt again, at temperature 0.

2026-11-11-nvidia-snapshot.lesson: Before a language model can answer, it must read its prompt, and it stores what it read in a KV cache. Reading a long prompt is slow on an ordinary computer. NVIDIA Snapshot saves a whole warmed-up GPU process and restores it in seconds instead of minutes. The same idea works on a laptop at a smaller scale: save the KV cache of a prompt you always use, and load it next time instead of reading the prompt again.
terms: starting a program from nothing, paying for every step of its setup
a saved copy of a running program's state, from which it can resume
what a language model keeps of the text it has read, so it does not read it again
quiz: Why must a restored KV cache be keyed by the model and the exact prompt tokens?
A cache is only valid for the model that made it and the text it read; any change in either makes it wrong.
Why does a small local model gain less from saving a whole process than a GPU server does?
It loads in about a second with nothing to compile, so the slow part left is reading long prompts.

build.why: Find secrets your agent's code can read directly: every one of them can end up in a log or a prompt.
Try OpenShell on Linux or macOS: it installs a command line and a local gateway, then creates an empty sandbox. This installs software.
build.cmd: curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/main/install.sh | sh && openshell sandbox create --name demo

build.why: List what your agent may reach today: files, hosts, tools. A policy starts from that list, with everything else denied.

2026-11-11-nvidia-openshell.lesson: An AI agent is useful because it can act: read files, run code, call services. The danger is that a model's output decides what it does, and that output can be manipulated. OpenShell puts the rules outside the agent: the operating system limits what files and network it can touch, a supervisor checks each request, and real passwords are added only when a request goes to an approved place, so the agent never holds them. A prover can show what a change of rules would newly allow before anyone accepts it.
terms: a confined place where a program runs without reaching the rest of the machine
nothing is allowed unless a rule allows it
a trusted part adds the secret to a request, so the program never sees it
quiz: Why enforce rules outside the agent's process rather than inside it?
Code inside the process, including code a model wrote, could change or skip the checks; a boundary outside it cannot be reached.
What does an agent gain from never holding a real credential?
Nothing it writes, logs or is tricked into saying can contain the secret, because it never had it.

build.why: Scan the skill before you install it: a skill runs with your agent's trust. This reads the repository and installs nothing.
Add the A2UI skills to your coding agent, so it can write A2UI screens. This installs files in your project.
List the components your app would let an agent use: that list is your locked catalog, and anything outside it is refused.
Check a screen before a user sees it: does every button say what it does?

2026-11-11-a2ui-1-0.lesson: Most AI agents answer with text, even when a form or a chart would serve the user better. A2UI lets an agent answer with a screen. The agent does not send code: it sends a description built only from components the app has approved, and the app draws them with its own buttons, charts and fields. A protocol makes the screen possible; whether the screen is clear and usable still has to be checked, which is what a design law like Zayn's is for.
terms: a user interface composed by an AI for one request, instead of designed in advance
the list of components an app allows an agent to use
the part of an app that turns a description into what is drawn on screen
quiz: Why does A2UI send data and not code?
Data can only use the components the app approved; code could do anything the app can do.
What does a locked catalog leave unchecked?
Whether the screen built from approved parts is clear: a button without a verb or a confusing flow is still made of approved parts.

build.why: Install SkillSpector as a command-line tool. This installs software.
Scan a skill before installing it, with the static checks only: no model and no key needed.
Scan the skills already in your project, and keep the report for review or continuous integration. This writes a file.

2026-11-12-nvidia-skillspector.lesson: A skill is a set of instructions, sometimes with scripts, that a coding agent installs and then follows as if you had written it. A skill can hide instructions that make the agent leak files, call unknown servers or ignore its rules. SkillSpector reads a skill before you install it and looks for 71 known risky patterns, then gives a risk score. Scanning first is the same habit as reading a package before you depend on it.
terms: a folder of instructions and scripts that a coding agent loads and follows
text written to make a model follow the writer's instructions instead of yours
a standard format for the findings of code scanners, read by CI systems and editors
quiz: Why is a skill riskier than an ordinary document?
The agent acts on it with your permissions: running commands, reading files, calling services.
What does the --no-llm option keep and what does it drop?
It keeps the fast static checks, which need no model or key, and drops the model's judgement of meaning.

build.why: Fetch ARC's open weights to read its configuration and heads. This downloads about a gigabyte.
The utility policy in one line: value a success, subtract what the step will cost, keep the best candidate.
build.cmd: best = max(models, key=lambda m: V * p_success[m] - expected_cost[m])

build.why: Local first: stay on your own model when it is confident, escalate only the hard steps.
build.cmd: answer = small(q) if small.top_probability(q) >= 0.85 else large(q)

2026-11-12-rayline-arc.lesson: An agent makes many calls, and they are not equally hard. A router is a small model that looks at each step and predicts which of the available models will succeed at it and what that will cost; a policy then picks the cheapest model likely to succeed. ARC does this with an open 0.8B model. Its prefer-local policy keeps a step on your own machine whenever the local model is predicted to succeed, and sends only the rest to a larger model. The same idea works between two local models when the small one says how sure it is.
terms: a component that chooses which model handles a request
sending a step to a stronger model only when the first one is likely to fail
a confidence that matches how often the answer is right
quiz: Why does a router predict cost separately from success?
Prices differ between applications, so the same prediction of tokens can be priced with each application's own rates.
What must be true before a small model's confidence can decide escalation?
Its confidence must be calibrated: when it says 0.9 it must be right about nine times in ten, which a golden set can check.

build.why: See what a model costs at each precision: parameters times bits per weight, divided by eight, gives bytes.
Make a smaller GGUF file from a larger one with llama.cpp, then compare both on your own test set before you switch.
LittleBit's layer in one line: two matrices of signs, scaled per row, per rank and per column.
build.cmd: y = ((((x * g) @ V_sign) * l) @ U_sign.T) * h

2026-11-12-samsung-littlebit.lesson: A model's size in memory is its number of weights times the bits used for each. Ordinary compression stores each weight in 4 or 8 bits. LittleBit goes below one bit per weight: it rewrites each weight matrix as two thin matrices of plus and minus signs with a few scales, then retrains them to imitate the original model. The model becomes many times smaller, and it answers less well, more so for small models. Whether a smaller file is good enough is a question your own tests must answer.
terms: the average storage for one model parameter; 16 for the usual format, 4 for common compressed files
storing weights with fewer bits than they were trained with
how surprised a model is by real text; lower is better
quiz: Why does a 0.1-bit model need retraining while a 4-bit file does not?
At 4 bits the rounded weights stay close to the originals; below one bit the matrix must be rebuilt, and only training can make the new one behave like the old.
Which loses more from aggressive compression, a 1B model or a 13B model?
Usually the 1B model, because each of its fewer weights carries more of what it knows.

build.why: Try the base model on one printed English line. This downloads about 250 MB.
build.cmd: python -c "from transformers import TrOCRProcessor, VisionEncoderDecoderModel; from PIL import Image; p=TrOCRProcessor.from_pretrained('microsoft/trocr-small-printed'); m=VisionEncoderDecoderModel.from_pretrained('microsoft/trocr-small-printed'); print(p.batch_decode(m.generate(p(Image.open('line.png').convert('RGB'), return_tensors='pt').pixel_values), skip_special_tokens=True)[0])"

build.why: Make a training picture from text: draw a word with a font, then damage it the way a camera or a scanner would.
Keep some words out of training, and test only on those: that shows the model reads letters and does more than recall words.

2026-11-13-trocr-arabic-synthetic.lesson: A text recogniser learns a script from pictures of text, and those pictures can be made by a program: take a list of words, draw each one in many fonts, and add blur, tilt and noise. One engineer taught a small English model to read Arabic this way in 80 minutes on one graphics card. The honest test is on words the model never saw in training; a high score there means it learned the letters and how they join. What the training pictures leave out, such as digits or punctuation, the model does not learn.
terms: continuing the training of an existing model on new examples
training examples a program generates, here pictures drawn from text
kept out of training so that it can serve as an honest test
quiz: Why test on words that were kept out of training?
A model can memorise the pictures of words it was shown; only unseen words show whether it reads letters.
A recogniser drops every digit it meets. What is the first thing to check?
Whether its training pictures contained digits; a model does not learn shapes it was never shown.

build.why: Read which version of the library your application was built with.
Pin the version you tested, by its tag, so that every build of your application uses the same library.
Before an upgrade, compare the two numbers: same first number, rebuild and run your tests; a new first number, read the release notes first.
build.cmd: 1.0.0 -> 1.4.2 : rebuild and test        1.4.2 -> 2.0.0 : read what changed

2026-11-13-llama-cpp-v1.lesson: A library's version number can be a promise. Under semantic versioning the number has three parts: the first changes when the library breaks something your code calls, the second when it adds something, the third when it fixes a bug. llama.cpp and ggml, the libraries most local AI applications run on, adopted this rule at version 1.0.0, after removing the old functions they had marked for removal. An application that keeps its own copy of a library writes down exactly which version it took, and its own tests decide whether a newer one is accepted.
terms: a rule that gives each of the three parts of a version number a meaning: breaking change, new feature, bug fix
the functions of a library that another program is allowed to call
still present, and announced as due for removal
keeping a copy of a library's source inside your own project, at a version you chose
quiz: Your application uses a library at 1.2.0 and version 1.5.0 appears. What does the number promise?
The functions you call still work the same way; new ones were added. Rebuild and run your tests.
Why does a project remove its deprecated functions just before version 1.0.0?
After 1.0.0 a removal breaks the promise and forces a version 2; removing them first lets the stable line start clean.

build.why: Watch your GPU while a model answers: the first column is the share of time a program occupied it, the second the share of time its memory was being read or written.
See which programs are computing on the GPU right now. Two at once on a small card compete for it.
Compute your card's ratio: operations per second it can do, divided by bytes per second its memory delivers. A task that does fewer operations per byte than this is waiting on memory.

2026-11-14-openinfer-gpu-os.lesson: A GPU has two speed limits: how fast it can calculate, and how fast its memory can deliver the numbers to calculate with. When a language model writes a token it reads all of its weights and does only a little arithmetic on each one, so the memory limit is reached first and the calculating units wait. A utilisation gauge shows the GPU as busy during that wait, because a program is occupying it. One company measured the calculating units active only 6 to 11% of the time on large models, and proposes to lend the waiting time to other work in very short pieces, the way an operating system shares a processor among programs.
terms: how many bytes per second a chip's memory can deliver to its calculating units
the share of time a program occupied the GPU, whatever the chip did in that time
the part of a system that decides which work uses a resource, and when
one pass through the model that produces the next token
quiz: A gauge shows 95% GPU utilisation while a model generates text. Does that mean the arithmetic units are nearly full?
No. It means a program occupied the GPU 95% of the time; the arithmetic can sit waiting for memory during most of it.
Why does generating text wait on memory?
Each token reads every weight of the model once and does only a few operations on each, so memory delivery is the slower of the two limits.

build.why: A gateway is one address your applications call; it forwards each request to a model. Here the application names a model and never learns which machine answers.
Mark a request as background work, so that it waits when people are being served.
Keep a project's requests on your own machines: a model served outside is then refused, as a fallback too.

2026-11-14-llmgw-gateway.lesson: When many programs and people share one language model, something has to stand in front of it and decide three things: who may call it, whose call goes first, and where a call may run. That something is called a gateway. Its simplest and most useful rule is the queue: requests from a waiting person go ahead, and background jobs wait their turn. One gateway reports that a person's answer took 1.24 times its usual time while 500 background jobs ran, and 58 times as long with the rule turned off. A second rule keeps data at home: a project marked as resident is refused any model outside the building.
terms: a program that receives every request for a service and decides how each one is served
deciding which requests start now and which wait, so that the urgent ones stay fast
one group of users of a shared service, with its own keys, limits and data
a rule about the place where data may be stored and processed
quiz: Ten agents and one person share a single model. Which request should be served first, and why?
The person's: a person is waiting, and background agents lose little by waiting a few seconds.
A project must keep its data on its own machines. Why must the rule also cover the fallback model?
A fallback is used when the first model fails; if it runs outside, the data leaves at exactly the moment nobody is watching.

build.why: See the cache at work with llama.cpp: save what the model has read of a long instruction, so that the next run starts from it.
Run again with the same file: the model restores its reading of the instruction and reads only what is new.
Name each saved reading by a hash of the model and the text, so that a cache is never restored into another model or after another text.

2026-11-14-google-tpu-sync.lesson: A language model reads a prompt once, from left to right, and keeps a working memory of what it read, called the key-value cache. Reading is the slow part; if the next prompt starts with the same text, the model can reuse that memory and read only the rest. This memory is large, so a system has to decide where each one lives: in the fastest memory beside the chip, in ordinary memory, on disk, or on another machine. Google's TPU Sync moves it between those levels without converting it, and reports the time to move it falling from seconds to about 230 milliseconds. The same idea works on a laptop with a file on disk.
terms: the working memory a model keeps of the text it has already read

quiz: Two prompts share their first 2,000 tokens. What can the model reuse for the second one?
Its key-value cache for those 2,000 tokens; it then reads only the tokens that differ.
Why must a saved cache be keyed by the model as well as by the text?
The cache holds that model's own internal numbers; another model, or another version of it, cannot use them.
